item.statement: Fewer people call themselves atheists after a DMT 'being' encounter, and after drug-free 'God' encounters too.
item.why: Among people who'd had such meetings, 28 in 100 recalled being atheists before a DMT encounter and 10 in 100 said they were now, and the share fell without drugs too. But they were recalling old beliefs years later.

lines.short: Mostly a being, a guide, a spirit or an alien. 69 in 100 said it gave them a message. People who said they'd met God without drugs told similar stories.
lines.but: Only people who'd had such a meeting took part, so we can't tell how often it happens.
how: In 2018, 2,561 adults described their most memorable meeting with a being after smoking or vaping DMT. Looking back, 65 in 100 judged it more real than everyday life.
On DMT, most said the being seemed conscious, intelligent and kind. Still, 41 in 100 felt fear at some point.
It's not just DMT. Of 809 people who said they met God or a higher power without drugs, 86 in 100 called it kind. 78 in 100 said they got a message.
28 in 100 recalled being atheists before the meeting, and 10 in 100 said they were now. Without drugs, the share fell too. But people recalled their old beliefs years later.

item.statement: Other people's cannabis smoke can never make you fail a urine drug test.
item.why: After an hour in a sealed, smoky room, 1 of 18 people who didn't smoke went over the US government's workplace limit, and 12 tested positive at least once at a lower limit some private tests use. That was one small lab test, mostly in thick smoke, not everyday smoke.

lines.short: Rarely at the US government's workplace limit: after an hour in a smoky sealed room, 1 of 18 people who didn't smoke went over it. At a lower limit, 12 did.
lines.but: One small lab test in a sealed room, mostly in thick smoke; everyday smoke wasn't tested.
how: In a sealed room about 3 by 4 metres, 6 people smoked cannabis freely for an hour. 6 people who didn't smoke sat between them. This was done 3 times, each time with 6 new people sitting in: 18 in all.
Only 1 of 250 urine samples went over the US government's workplace limit. It did so on just 1 of 5 labs' tests.
Some private tests use a lower limit. There, 12 of the 18 tested positive at least once on at least one of 4 tests. A lab check would have confirmed it for 3 to 7, depending on the test.
A positive is a urine result: a THC breakdown product above a set level. It is not a measure of being high.

item.statement: In lab tests, fentanyl test strips often missed fentanyl that was really there.
item.why: Strips showed fentanyl in 104 of 106 police-seized samples that had it. But trained lab staff did the tests, mostly with one brand, and testing at home wasn't studied.

lines.short: Almost always, in lab tests: 98 in 100 seized drug samples with fentanyl showed it on the strip.
lines.but: Lab staff did these tests, mostly with one brand. Testing at home was not studied.
how: Two labs tested strips on 106 police-seized drug samples that had fentanyl. The strips showed it in 104.
A lab machine had already found fentanyl in all of these samples. Samples with very little fentanyl were not tested this way.
Strips can find very small amounts of fentanyl. But the smallest amount found differed up to 25 times between studies and batches.
It also depended on how a faint line was read. Trained staff did all of these tests.

item.statement: In older US surveys, about 9 in 100 people who ever tried cannabis became dependent.
item.why: In the first survey, that was fewer than for tobacco, heroin, cocaine or alcohol. The surveys ran from 1990 to 2005 and used a narrower definition; newer US figures that count milder cases are higher.

lines.short: About 9 in 100 people who ever tried it, in two older US surveys.
lines.but: The surveys are from 1990 to 2005 and used a narrower definition than today's.
how: A US survey in 1990 to 1992 asked about 8,000 people aged 15 to 54 about drug use and dependence.
Of those who had ever used cannabis, even once, about 9 in 100 had been dependent at some point: fewer than for tobacco, heroin, cocaine or alcohol.
A second US survey, in 2001 to 2005, estimated about 9 in 100 over a lifetime; half of those who became dependent did so within about 5 years of first use.
Newer US figures are higher, about 3 in 10, but they count milder cases and only people who used in the past year.

item.statement: If a friend took the same MDMA and didn't overheat, you won't either.
item.why: Nobody can yet say why some people get hotter than others: in one case of severe overheating, a friend who took the same MDMA didn't overheat. That's second-hand, from one review of small studies and cases.

lines.short: Nobody can yet say why some people get hotter than others with MDMA.
lines.but: This is second-hand, from one review of small studies. They couldn't tell heat, dancing and crowds apart.
how: In small lab studies of people at rest, body temperature rose about 0.4 degrees on average at medium doses and 0.7 at higher ones; one person in a group of 8 went up 1.9.
At clubs and parties the average rise ran from 0.2 to 1.6 degrees. But the review reports no comparison of amounts, dancing, room heat or crowds, so which matters is unknown.

Severe overheating (40 degrees and up, sometimes fatal) is known from hospital cases. In one UK report, blood levels didn't suggest high doses. In another case, a friend who took the same MDMA didn't overheat.
People also feel it differently: in one survey, 16 in 100 people who take ecstasy did not feel hot.

item.statement: All antidepressants carry about the same serotonin risk when mixed with ecstasy.
item.why: One 2007 review ranked MAOI antidepressants highest and SSRI-type antidepressants lower. That's the authors' judgment from reports and how the drugs work; no study counted how often each mix causes harm.

lines.short: One 2007 review ranked drugs by serotonin risk with ecstasy: MAOIs highest, SSRIs lower.
lines.but: This is the authors' judgment from reports and how the drugs work, not from counts of people.
how: Lower risk, the review says: SSRI-type antidepressants and a few painkillers and cough medicines, which it says weaken ecstasy's effects.
Middle: stimulants such as amphetamine and cocaine, and supplements such as tryptophan. Highest: MAOI antidepressants.
Deaths from serotonin syndrome with ecstasy alone are rare, the review says, but harm is more likely with other drugs that act on serotonin.
No study counted how often each mix causes harm. Some people feel little from an amount of ecstasy and take more; no study measured what that does to the risk.

item.statement: In a UK expert ranking of 20 drugs, tobacco scored zero for deaths like overdose.
item.why: Lung cancer was counted elsewhere, and the authors agreed tobacco probably kills more than the other 19 drugs combined. The scores are one panel's views, not measures.

lines.short: Experts have tried: a UK panel ranked alcohol most harmful overall, mostly for harm to other people. For the person using, crack, heroin and meth scored worst.
lines.but: The scores are one panel's views, not measures, and alcohol's top score partly reflects how many people drink.
how: In 2010, experts scored 20 drugs on 16 harms in one day. A 2007 expert ranking put legal alcohol and tobacco above LSD and ecstasy.
Alcohol scored 72 of 100, 46 of them for harm to others. Critics say one score mixes harm per person with how many people use.
Tobacco scored zero for deaths like overdose. Lung cancer was counted elsewhere. The authors agreed it probably kills more than the other 19 drugs combined.
In an online survey, 1,501 people rated drug harms much like experts did. Of the 603 allowed to rate heroin, 467 had never used it.

item.statement: In lab tests, men told their drink had vodka drank more, whatever was really in it.
item.why: They drank about twice as much in 15 minutes, while real vodka made no clear difference to how much they drank. These were lab tests from the 1970s and 1980s, with low blood alcohol.

lines.short: In lab tests, partly: believing they drank alcohol made men drink more.
lines.but: Lab tests from the 1970s and 1980s; the drinking test lasted 15 minutes, with low blood alcohol.
how: 64 men were told at random that their drink had vodka or not, and were given vodka or not, also at random. Half had a history of drinking problems.
Men told it had vodka drank about twice as much in 15 minutes, whatever was really in the glass. Real vodka made no clear difference to how much they drank.
Across 36 similar experiments, believing you had drunk alcohol went with more drinking, but not with changes in mood or memory. Sexual arousal rose on average, but that varied a lot between studies.
The alcohol itself, not the belief, affected memory, coordination, body sensations and mood. Blood alcohol in the drinking study stayed low, so heavier drinking may differ.

item.statement: Colour test kits for MDMA are easy to read, even for first-timers.
item.why: In one small 2003 lab study, two people new to the kit made many mistakes: one missed both MDMA samples, and the other called four other drugs MDMA. Lab experts got MDMA right.

lines.short: In a lab, experts got MDMA right. Two first-time testers made many mistakes.
lines.but: One small lab study from 2003, with a kit and pills of that time.
how: Three lab experts read all 35 samples with MDMA as positive, and nearly all of the 4 without MDMA as negative.
Seven MDMA samples also had another drug, like caffeine or amphetamine. The colour looked the same.
Two people new to the kit tested 8 known drugs. One missed both MDMA samples. The other called four other drugs MDMA.
A review says MDA and MDEA, drugs close to MDMA, give a similar colour. It adds that, read by eye, the tests do not show how much MDMA a pill holds.

item.statement: People who microdose can't tell a real microdose from a dummy capsule.
item.why: In trials, people guessed right about 7 times in 10, and their ratings followed what they believed they'd taken. Feeling an effect may have shaped that belief.

lines.short: In two trials, people could feel a magic mushroom or LSD microdose on the day. But their mood and thinking were not clearly better than with a dummy capsule.
lines.but: Only a small one-week trial used just magic mushrooms; the bigger one was mostly LSD, and neither lasted months.
how: In Argentina, 34 people took magic mushroom capsules one week and look-alike capsules of an ordinary mushroom another. Mood and creativity did not improve.
A bigger study: 240 people mixed their own microdoses, mostly LSD, with empty capsules. After 4 weeks, the dummy group was not clearly worse off.
People guessed right about 7 times in 10. Ratings followed what they believed they took, though feeling an effect may have shaped the belief.
Everyone in both studies took capsules, so neither can show it is all placebo. People might have got better anyway.

item.statement: When deaths were blamed on mephedrone, tests always found the drug in the body.
item.why: By October 2011, 128 deaths in the UK and nearby islands had been linked to it, and tests after death found none in 25. A negative test may miss earlier use, and a positive one doesn't prove cause.

lines.short: In 25 of 128 alleged deaths, tests after death found no mephedrone.
lines.but: A positive test does not prove cause. A negative test may miss earlier use.
how: By October 2011, 128 deaths in the UK and nearby islands had been linked to mephedrone; 13 results were still pending.
Of 62 deaths studied, mephedrone was the only substance found in 8. Other drugs were common.
One person died weeks later in hospital and had none found after death. Their earlier test evidence is not given.
The authors say tests and incomplete reporting may also miss deaths. They cannot give a death rate.

item.statement: There's one agreed way to count a death as a drug death.
item.why: Lists use different rules, some counting drug poisoning as the main cause and others drugs found in tests. In Norway, only about 49 in 100 deaths were on both of two lists, and in Sweden fewer than half.

lines.short: Different lists use different rules, so they do not always count the same deaths.
lines.but: The matching studies cover three places. The newest linked data are from 2012.
how: Some lists count drug poisoning as the main cause. Others count drugs found in tests, with age limits.
One death can be counted under several drugs. Finding a drug does not by itself show that it caused the death.
About 49 out of 100 people were on both lists in Norway. Fewer than half were on both in Sweden.
In New Mexico, about 89 out of 100 were on both lists. This study included other poisons too.

item.statement: Bupropion and modafinil have been shown to help people stop using meth.
item.why: Across five trials, about 1 in 5 had stopped by the end, whether on medicine or a dummy pill. The trials were small, so a modest benefit or harm can't be ruled out.

lines.short: Bupropion and modafinil did not help more people stop than a dummy pill.
lines.but: The trials were small, so a modest benefit or harm cannot be ruled out.
how: Putting five trials together: about 1 in 5 had stopped by the end, on medicine or on a dummy pill.
The trials were small and uneven, so a modest benefit or harm can't be ruled out.
A later review of bupropion found about a tenth fewer positive urine tests. This result is uncertain.

item.statement: A study found ketamine trips feel like near-death experiences.
item.why: Only words were compared: a computer checked the words in about 15,000 online trip reports against 625 near-death accounts. Nobody showed the experiences themselves feel alike.

lines.short: More than for any other drug, going by the words alone: of 165 drugs, ketamine trip reports read most like near-death accounts. Salvia and LSD came close behind.
lines.but: Only words were compared. Nobody showed the trips and the near-death experiences feel alike.
how: Researchers took about 15,000 drug reports from the Erowid website. A computer compared their words with 625 near-death accounts.
Ketamine came first with the main settings, and with about 4 in 5 of all the settings tried. On average it led LSD only narrowly, and lower down, drugs swapped places.
The near-death accounts were written about 20 years after the event, on average, and some were linked to anaesthesia or drug use. Nobody checked what the online writers took, or how much.
Some think the brain releases a ketamine-like chemical near death. The authors say their study can't show that, though their summary says it supports the idea.

item.statement: MDMA therapy papers left out side effects that their own trial records listed.
item.why: More than half of the less serious problems in the trial records never made it into the papers, and neither did 4 of 13 serious ones, all 4 in people on MDMA. Most studies also noted only problems people raised themselves.

lines.short: Common ones were a tight jaw, anxiety, less appetite, feeling sick and sweating. They happened during sessions and in the week after. Most were mild to moderate and soon passed.
lines.but: The record is patchy. Most studies only noted problems people raised themselves. Some never reached the papers, and later risks are barely known.
how: These effects were more common than with a dummy pill or a very small dose.
In one small trial in people with a serious illness, 11 of 13 on MDMA had a tight jaw, against 1 of 5 on a dummy pill.
One review found one serious problem linked to MDMA. Extra heartbeats the person already had got more frequent. They were watched overnight in hospital.
Trial records listed problems the papers left out. That was more than half of the less serious ones, and 4 of 13 serious ones. All 4 were in people on MDMA.

item.statement: The review that found DARE made no difference only tested the original classes, not the 2001 rebuild.
item.why: All 11 studies in the 2004 review, covering over 11,000 students, looked at the original classes; the version rebuilt in 2001 wasn't part of it. So it says nothing either way about the newer classes.

lines.short: No. Across 11 studies of the original DARE school classes, kids who had DARE said they used alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs about as much as kids who didn't.
lines.but: Only the original classes were tested: DARE was rebuilt in 2001, and that version wasn't part of this review.
how: A 2004 review combined 11 studies, published 1991 to 2002, of 11,505 students in grades 5 to 12, comparing those who had DARE with those who didn't.
Students who had DARE said they used alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs about as much as others. The studies checked from right after the classes to 10 years later.
In 8 of the 11 studies, the result couldn't be told apart from no difference. Two small ones found less use with DARE; the biggest, of 2,878 students, found slightly more.
Four results, including the only 10-year one, weren't worked out but filled in as zero.

item.statement: Most people who start using cocaine are hooked within a year.
item.why: In US surveys, about 5 in 100 people who had used only powder were dependent within a year of starting, and about 22 in 100 of those who went on to crack. People answered once, so the surveys can't show crack itself made the difference.

lines.short: Within a year of starting, about 5 in 100 who used only powder were dependent; 22 in 100 who went on to crack.
lines.but: People answered once, about themselves. The survey cannot show that crack itself made the difference.
how: US surveys from 2002 to 2016 asked people who had first used cocaine less than a year before.
About 5 in 100 of those who had used only powder met the criteria for cocaine dependence. So did about 22 in 100 of those who had gone on to crack.
In both groups the most common problem was wanting or trying to cut down or stop: about 45 in 100 and 58 in 100.
People who go on to crack may differ to begin with, and some may already have had problems with powder. The survey did not ask which form caused a problem.

item.statement: Among people who got ill after MDMA, low blood salt was more common in women than men.
item.why: In one poison-centre study, 52 in 100 women tested had low blood salt, against 22 in 100 men. It counted only people ill enough to be reported and tested, so it can't say who's most at risk among everyone who takes MDMA.

lines.short: Yes, among people who got ill: 52 in 100 women tested had low blood salt, against 22 in 100 men, in one poison-centre study.
lines.but: It counts only people ill enough to be reported and tested, so it can't say who's most at risk among everyone who takes MDMA.
how: Only 188 of 545 people in California poison-centre records had a blood salt test. Of 105 women tested, 55 had a low level; of 83 men, 18 did.
Women with a low level were also more likely to have fits or coma than women without one; in men the numbers were too small to tell.
A UK group (10 of 17 were women) and a review of published cases (more than 85 in 100 were female) point the same way, but the review's cases overlap with the California ones.
A review describes 8 women and 8 men given the same MDMA amount: a marker of a water-holding hormone rose only in women, with no clear difference reported in the hormone or blood salt.

item.statement: Cannabis medicines work much better than a dummy medicine for long-lasting pain.
item.why: In combined trials, pain was only about half a point lower out of 10 than with a dummy medicine. The trials were short, mostly tested one mouth spray, and many had weaknesses.

lines.short: Slightly: about half a point less pain out of 10 than with a dummy medicine.
lines.but: The trials were short, mostly tested one mouth spray, and many had weaknesses.
how: Researchers combined trials. People with long-lasting pain got a cannabis medicine or a dummy medicine (placebo).
Pain scores were about half a point lower out of 10 with the medicine.
37 in 100 people on the medicine and 31 in 100 on the dummy had their pain cut by at least 30%; this difference may be due to chance.
Most of the combined trials tested a mouth spray with THC and CBD, and none lasted more than 15 weeks.

item.statement: Teens who use the most cannabis are a bit more likely to be depressed as young adults.
item.why: Across seven long-term studies, teens in the highest-use group had about 1.4 times the odds of depression as young adults. That's a link, not proof: other differences between the teens may explain it.

lines.short: Teens who used cannabis the most were a bit more often depressed later than teens who didn't.
lines.but: These studies can't show that cannabis caused it; other differences between the teens may explain it.
how: Seven long-term studies followed teens who did and did not use cannabis until they were young adults.
Teens in the highest-use group had about 1.4 times the odds of depression as young adults. The studies did not say how many in 100 became depressed.
The studies took into account how depressed or anxious the teens were at the start, but not always tobacco or other drugs.
Anxiety did not clearly differ, but only three studies measured it.

item.statement: Brain scans prove that ecstasy destroys serotonin nerve cells.
item.why: Four teams found less of a serotonin marker in the outer brain of people who use ecstasy, but less marker can also mean cells make less of it, not that cells are gone. Nobody was scanned before they started, and these groups also used more other drugs.

lines.short: Scans show less of a serotonin marker in people who use ecstasy.
lines.but: Nobody in these studies was scanned before they started, and these groups also used more other drugs.
how: The marker sits on the endings of serotonin nerve cells in the brain.
Four teams used the same scan and all found less of it in the outer brain.
Deeper parts of the brain mostly looked the same as in other people.
Less marker can also mean cells make less of it, not that cells are gone.

item.statement: A psychedelic flashback means reliving the whole trip for hours.
item.why: In Swiss lab studies of LSD and psilocybin, a flashback was usually a few seconds of changed seeing, mostly in the days after, and most people didn't mind it. These were healthy, screened volunteers, with no drug-free group to compare.

lines.short: About 1 in 11 lab volunteers reported a short flashback, mostly in the days after.
lines.but: These were healthy, screened volunteers in labs, with no drug-free group to compare.
how: 142 healthy adults took LSD, psilocybin or both in lab studies in Switzerland.
At the end, 13 said they had had a flashback, usually a few seconds of changed seeing.
Most did not mind it; 2 people were upset by it.
Nobody was found to have the long-lasting vision condition doctors call HPPD.

item.statement: Only a few psychiatric medicines have been tested together with MDMA in studies.
item.why: Each was tested once, in 14 to 16 healthy people, and results differed: with MDMA, the antipsychotic haloperidol lowered well-being and raised anxiety. For several others, a 2022 review found no controlled study at all.

lines.short: Few other psychiatric medicines were tested with MDMA, and the results differ by medicine.
lines.but: Each was tested once in 14 to 16 healthy people, and the results come second-hand from a 2022 review.
how: Haloperidol, an antipsychotic, did not change heart rate or blood pressure. It lowered well-being by about 31 percent and raised anxiety by about 47 percent.
Methylphenidate, a stimulant, delayed MDMA's peak by about 46 percent. Carvedilol, a heart medicine, cut the rise in heart rate by about 79 percent.
The review found no controlled study of MAOIs, lithium or benzodiazepines with MDMA.
A slow start, as with methylphenidate, can leave a person feeling little, and some people then take more. No trial tested what happens then.

item.statement: Bladder problems linked to ketamine never ease, even after people stop using it.
item.why: In one survey, 128 of 251 people who described how their symptoms changed said they eased after stopping. No study has compared people who stopped with people who kept using, though.

lines.short: Ketamine is linked to bladder problems seen in over 4,000 patients. In one survey, about 1 in 4 people who used it blamed it for urine problems.
lines.but: No study compared how often people who use ketamine and people who don't get these problems. So none can show ketamine caused them.
how: In over 4,000 patients seen by doctors, mostly in Asia, about 77 in 100 needed to pee often and 60 in 100 had bladder pain.
In about 3 in 10 of these patients, urine had backed up and swollen a kidney. About 8 in 100 had weaker kidney function.
The survey was online, mostly in the UK: 1,285 people who had used ketamine in the past year. Those who used more reported more symptoms.
Of 251 people who described how symptoms changed, 128 said they eased after stopping. No study compared people who stopped with those who kept using.

item.statement: Drinking alcohol was estimated to cause about 4 in 100 new cancers worldwide in 2020.
item.why: A model put it at 741,000 new cancers, about 6 in 100 in men and 2 in 100 in women, led by gullet, liver, breast and bowel cancer. It's a computer estimate built on risks from studies of groups, not a count.

lines.short: A model estimated that drinking caused about 4 in 100 new cancers worldwide in 2020.
lines.but: It is a computer estimate, not a count. It applies risks from studies of groups of people to every country.
how: Researchers combined how much people drink in each country with cancer risks from earlier studies. They compared this with a world where no one had ever drunk.
They estimated 741,000 new cancers in 2020: about 6 in 100 new cancers in men and 2 in 100 in women. Gullet, liver, breast and bowel cancer made up the most.
Most were linked to more than 20 g of alcohol a day, about two drinks. About 103,000 were linked to less than that.
The model counted only harms, for the cancers an international agency lists. An older model by an overlapping team estimated 487,000 cancer deaths from alcohol in 2004.

item.statement: Drinking coffee raises your risk of lung cancer.
item.why: A link between coffee and lung cancer disappeared in people who had never smoked: people who smoke tend to drink more coffee. These studies only watched people.

lines.short: Mostly better: in studies that followed people for years, people who drank coffee died a bit less often. In pregnancy, and for women's bones, the links went the other way.
lines.but: These studies only watched people, and gene studies found no sign that coffee itself lowers the risk of dying.
how: A big review gathered the research on coffee and health. Most of it came from studies that followed people for years.
People who drank coffee had lower rates of death, heart disease, type 2 diabetes and, most of all, liver disease.
In pregnancy, more coffee was linked to low birth weight and losing the pregnancy. Women who drank more had more fractures; men had fewer.
A link between coffee and lung cancer disappeared in people who had never smoked; people who smoke tend to drink more coffee.

item.statement: Headaches from skipping caffeine come from expecting them, not from the missing caffeine.
item.why: Before a small operation, people who drank lots of caffeine got caffeine or identical dummy pills, and neither they nor the doctor checking symptoms knew which. By evening, 10 of 20 on dummy pills had a headache and none on caffeine did, though only 40 patients took part and surgery can also cause headaches.

lines.short: Without their usual caffeine, half got a headache by evening; people given caffeine pills did not.
lines.but: Only 40 hospital patients took part, and surgery itself can also cause headaches.
how: 40 people who drank lots of caffeine had to stop it before a small operation.
Half got caffeine pills and half got identical dummy pills, and neither the patients nor the doctor checking symptoms knew which.
By evening, 10 of the 20 with dummy pills had a headache, and none with caffeine.

item.statement: Babies whose mothers used cannabis in pregnancy went to newborn intensive care more often.
item.why: Across 19 studies, mostly from before 2000, these babies were also about 109 grams lighter. But many mothers also smoked or drank, and most studies couldn't tell that apart from cannabis.

lines.short: Babies were a bit lighter, and more of them went to intensive care after birth.
lines.but: Many mothers also smoked or drank. Most studies could not tell this apart from cannabis.
how: Researchers combined 19 studies, mostly from before 2000. They compared babies of mothers who did and did not use cannabis while pregnant.
Babies of mothers who used cannabis weighed about 109 grams less. More of them went to newborn intensive care.
It is not clear whether they were born early more often. Birth defects and deaths around birth were not clearly more common.
Most studies did not keep tobacco and alcohol apart from cannabis. So they cannot show that cannabis caused the differences.

item.statement: Kratom shows up in a large share of US overdose deaths.
item.why: In 27 US states in 2016–17, kratom was found in 152 of 27,338 overdose deaths, about 6 in 1,000. Testing for kratom varied and wasn't recorded, so some deaths with it were probably missed.

lines.short: Kratom turned up in about 6 of every 1,000 overdose deaths in 27 US states in 2016–17. It was almost always found with other drugs.
lines.but: Testing for kratom varied and was not recorded, so some deaths with kratom were probably missed.
how: A CDC system gathered 27,338 overdose deaths from 27 US states, July 2016 to December 2017. Kratom was found in 152.
Kratom was named as a cause in 91 deaths. Other drugs turned up in 84 of them; fentanyl was named as a cause in 51.
Only 7 deaths had kratom as the only drug found. Even then, the report says other drugs cannot be ruled out.
The system counts mostly deaths where opioids played a part. With no count of people who use kratom, there is no death rate.

item.statement: Most people who use meth end up diagnosed with psychosis.
item.why: In Taiwan, an estimated 4 in 100 adults arrested for using amphetamine-type drugs got a psychosis diagnosis within 10 years, against under 1 in 100 with no drug record. No study has settled which comes first.

lines.short: Psychotic symptoms are more common in people who use meth, most of all in those who use it often.
lines.but: No study has settled which comes first.
how: In studies mostly in treatment, hospitals or prisons, a meth or amphetamine use disorder went with about 2.5 times the odds of psychosis.
In New Zealand, about 1,000 people followed from birth: use went with slightly more psychotic experiences.
In Taiwan, an estimated 4 in 100 adults arrested for using amphetamine-type drugs got a psychosis diagnosis within 10 years. Among people with no drug record, it was under 1 in 100.
None of these studies shows which came first.

item.statement: The risk of dying is highest in the first week after leaving prison.
item.why: In death records of about 1.5 million people, days 2 to 7 after release carried about 1.5 to 2 times the risk of later weeks, and drug or alcohol poisoning was the top recorded cause. Tolerance was never measured, so the records can't say why.

lines.short: Yes. In the first week out, the risk of dying was about 1.5 to 2 times that of later weeks. Drug or alcohol poisoning was the top recorded cause.
lines.but: It's death records only: they don't name the drugs, and nobody measured tolerance, so the study can't say why.
how: Researchers used death records for about 1.5 million people who left prison or jail in eight countries, between 1980 and 2018.
16 of the 18 groups had records for each day. In them, the risk of dying in days 2 to 7 after release was about 1.5 to 2 times the risk in later weeks.
Drug or alcohol poisoning was the top recorded cause, in that first week and overall. Yet 91 in 100 of those deaths came after week 4, since people were followed for much longer than that.
The study had no information on drug use, treatment or tolerance. So it cannot say why the first week is riskier.

item.statement: A negative xylazine test strip means there's no xylazine.
item.why: With less xylazine than strips are made to find, only 6 of 28 samples read positive, against 37 of 38 with at least that much. That was one batch of strips, read in a lab, on residues from used equipment.

lines.short: Yes, if there's at least as much xylazine as they're made to find: 37 of 38 such samples read positive. With less, only 6 of 28 did.
lines.but: It's one batch of strips, read in a lab, on residues from used equipment, not powders or pills.
how: A lab tested 100 residue samples wiped from used syringes, bags and pill bottles, and checked them with a lab machine.
With enough xylazine, 37 of 38 read positive; with less, 6 of 28. That's 43 of all 66 with xylazine. None of 34 without it read positive.
In pure water, every strip read positive only from 2.5 times the amount the strip is made to find.
Lidocaine, a common cutting agent, also made strips read positive. At the one level tested, they didn't react to medetomidine. That's a similar drug used on animals.

item.statement: In a trial of psilocybin against an antidepressant, people expected nearly twice as much from psilocybin.
item.why: Allowing for those higher hopes, the team found no clear gap between psilocybin and escitalopram on any of six scales. With 59 people, the trial was too small to show the two work equally well.

lines.short: Not shown. In one trial of 59 people, psilocybin and the antidepressant escitalopram showed no clear difference in depression, at 6 weeks or 6 months.
lines.but: The trial was too small to show they work equally well, and people expected nearly twice as much from psilocybin.
how: At one London centre, 59 adults with depression got two psilocybin sessions, or 6 weeks of escitalopram pills plus two tiny psilocybin doses.
After 6 weeks, self-rated depression fell 8 points with psilocybin and 6 with escitalopram, on a 27-point scale: a gap that could be chance.
At 6 weeks, 57 in 100 were nearly free of symptoms with psilocybin and 28 with escitalopram, an extra result the authors drew no conclusions from. Six months on: 37 against 34.
People had higher hopes for psilocybin. Allowing for those hopes, the team found no clear gap on any of six scales.

item.statement: CBD products usually contain what their labels say.
item.why: In a 2016 US test of 84 CBD products sold online, only about 3 in 10 matched their CBD label, and about 1 in 5 also held THC. Shop products, or today's, may differ.

lines.short: Mostly not. Of 84 CBD products bought online in the US in 2016, only about 3 in 10 matched their CBD label. About 1 in 5 also held THC.
lines.but: One test of products bought online in 2016; products sold in shops, or today, may differ.
how: CBD is a substance from the cannabis plant. Researchers bought every CBD oil, tincture and vape liquid with a CBD label they found online.
A lab that did not know the labels tested them. 36 held more CBD than the label said, and 22 held less.
Vape liquids were most often wrong: 21 of 24 were off by more than a tenth, mostly holding more CBD than labelled.
No one took the products, and no urine was tested. So this can't say if they cause a high or a positive drug test.

item.statement: People who started using drugs at 13 or younger more often became dependent than later starters.
item.why: In a US survey of adults who'd used drugs at least 12 times, about 1 in 3 who started by 13 had been dependent, against about 1 in 7 who started at 21 or older. A big twin study found much of the link runs in families, so starting young isn't shown to be the cause.

lines.short: People who started young more often had drug or drinking problems later on.
lines.but: Studies can't show that starting young is the cause. Much of the link runs in families.
how: A 1992 US survey asked adults who had used drugs at least 12 times. About 1 in 3 who started at 13 or younger had been dependent on drugs. For those who started at 21 or older, it was about 1 in 7.

In New Zealand, children were asked about drinking and drugs at 13 and 15, not years later. At 32, 29 in 100 of those who used several times by 15, mostly alcohol, were dependent on alcohol or drugs. For teens with similar childhoods who had not, it was 15 in 100.
In Australian twins, the twin who started cannabis before 17 more often had drug problems by the study's rules. It was about 48 in 100, against 33 in 100 for the other twin.
A bigger twin study found the link was not strong, and much of it ran in families. Its authors think waiting longer to start would cut the risk only a little.

item.statement: Clonidine and lofexidine barely help with heroin withdrawal.
item.why: In three trials, about 19 in 100 on them had bad withdrawal, against about 59 in 100 on a dummy pill, and more finished treatment. But the trials were small and old, and none included people coming off fentanyl.

lines.short: Yes: compared with a dummy pill, fewer people had bad withdrawal and more finished treatment.
lines.but: Only three small, old trials, mostly in hospital, and none with people coming off fentanyl.
how: Three trials gave people coming off heroin either the medicine or a dummy pill, picked by chance.
Bad withdrawal happened to about 19 in 100 on the medicine and about 59 in 100 on the dummy pill.
About 56 in 100 finished treatment on the medicine, against 29 in 100 on the dummy pill.
The medicine made some people sleepy or dizzy and lowered their blood pressure.

item.statement: An SSRI antidepressant that dulls MDMA's effects also lowers MDMA levels in your blood.
item.why: In 12 men, the SSRI paroxetine lessened MDMA's rises in blood pressure, heart rate and pupil size, yet the MDMA peak in their blood was about 1 in 6 higher. Only healthy volunteers were tested, for a few days at most.

lines.short: An SSRI muted MDMA's effects in lab tests; with paroxetine, MDMA blood levels rose.
lines.but: Only 28 healthy volunteers were tested, for a few days at most, and no one was given more MDMA.
how: 16 volunteers rated MDMA's effects about 60 percent lower after citalopram; their blood levels were not measured.
In 12 men, paroxetine lessened the rises in the upper blood pressure number, heart rate and pupil size. Yet the MDMA peak in the blood was about 1 in 6 higher.
Feeling little can have many reasons: a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, bodies that differ, or a medicine that mutes the effect, as here.
No one was given more MDMA once its effects were muted, so what happens then is not known; the paroxetine authors suggest it could add risk.

item.statement: When MDMA is found in the blood of someone who died, it usually caused the death.
item.why: In 106 Australian coroners' cases with MDMA in the blood, 6 in 10 died of injuries, such as a crash. A blood test after death can't show who took what, when or why.

lines.short: Among 19 Australian deaths with MDMA and a risky mix, antidepressants, opioids and benzos were common.
lines.but: The 19 were picked for risky mixes, so the counts do not show how common any mix is.
how: In 14,682 coroners' cases (2002 to 2008), 106 had MDMA in the blood. Six in 10 of them died of injuries such as hanging or a crash, so MDMA in the blood does not show that it caused the death.
The authors rated 19 of the 106 as having a risky drug combination. Of those 19, 15 also had methamphetamine or amphetamine, 13 an antidepressant, 12 an opioid and 8 a benzodiazepine (benzo).
Four of them had moclobemide, an antidepressant of the MAO-inhibitor type. Three of those four showed signs of serotonin toxicity before they died.

A blood test after death cannot show who took what, when or why, and where the medicines came from was mostly unknown. A second-hand report of 75 UK deaths found other drugs, mostly opiates and sedatives, in 93 in 100.

item.statement: Cocaine with alcohol makes the heart beat faster than cocaine alone.
item.why: In 8 people on a hospital ward, heart rate averaged about 84 beats a minute with both, against 74 with cocaine alone. These small studies didn't measure heart attacks or rhythm problems.

lines.short: Together they make a new substance, cocaethylene, and hearts beat faster than with cocaine alone.
lines.but: Small hospital studies of 8 and 6 people. None measured heart attacks or rhythm problems.
how: Eight adults who already used both drugs took cocaine by the nose on a hospital ward. With alcohol, their heart rate averaged about 84 beats a minute, against 74 with cocaine alone.
There was also about 13 to 15 percent more cocaine in their blood, and cocaethylene, which the body makes only when both drugs are there and which leaves the blood more slowly than cocaine.

In a second study, cocaine went into a vein with alcohol. Cocaethylene formed again, but stayed at a small fraction of the cocaine level, and none of it appeared when cocaine was given without alcohol.

Cocaethylene has been found in people's blood after both drugs, including after deaths, but such tests cannot show what caused a death. In over 1,000 emergency-room tests, people positive for both drugs had no more heart problems than people positive for one.

item.statement: If a colour test shows MDMA, the pill has nothing else in it.
item.why: In one small 2003 lab study, seven MDMA samples that also held another drug, like caffeine or amphetamine, gave the same colour as MDMA alone. A review adds that drugs close to MDMA, like MDA, give a similar colour.

lines.short: In a lab, experts got MDMA right. Two first-time testers made many mistakes.
lines.but: One small lab study from 2003, with a kit and pills of that time.
how: Three lab experts read all 35 samples with MDMA as positive, and nearly all of the 4 without MDMA as negative.
Seven MDMA samples also had another drug, like caffeine or amphetamine. The colour looked the same.
Two people new to the kit tested 8 known drugs. One missed both MDMA samples. The other called four other drugs MDMA.
A review says MDA and MDEA, drugs close to MDMA, give a similar colour. It adds that, read by eye, the tests do not show how much MDMA a pill holds.

item.statement: In lab studies, meth made attention and memory clearly worse at the time.
item.why: In small lab studies, attention, memory and reaction time didn't get measurably worse. But small or moderate harm can't be ruled out, and binges weren't tested.

lines.short: In lab tests, single doses did not measurably worsen attention or memory.
lines.but: The studies were small, so small or moderate harm can't be ruled out. Binges were not tested.
how: Lab studies gave people mostly single doses.
Attention, memory and reaction time did not get measurably worse. On some tasks people did better.
The studies were small. The two main ones, and the review of the others, came from one research group.
Binges and long-term use were not tested.

item.statement: In UK methadone or buprenorphine treatment, people also prescribed benzos died of poisoning more often.
item.why: Poisoning deaths were about 1 in 100 people a year with a benzo prescription, against 1 in 200 without, even though those on benzos stayed in treatment longer. The study didn't allow for mental health, alcohol or street drug use.

lines.short: In UK methadone or buprenorphine treatment, benzo prescriptions were linked to more poisoning deaths.
lines.but: The study did not take mental health, alcohol or street drug use into account.
how: Poisoning deaths were about 1 in 100 people per year with a benzo prescription, and 1 in 200 without.
The link was stronger when benzo doses were above the highest dose the UK drug guide advises.
Sleeping tablets called z-drugs were also linked to poisoning deaths, though deaths were few.
People prescribed benzos stayed in treatment longer, but the link with poisoning deaths was still there.

item.statement: Fewer people went back to heavy drinking on naltrexone than on dummy pills.
item.why: About 46 in 100 on naltrexone went back to heavy drinking, against 54 in 100 on dummy pills; feeling sick, dizziness and vomiting were more common. Most were middle-aged men who had already stopped drinking and had counselling.

lines.short: On naltrexone, 46 in 100 went back to heavy drinking, against 54 on dummy pills.
lines.but: Most people in the trials were middle-aged men who had already stopped drinking and had counselling.
how: Naltrexone is a tablet. Dozens of trials gave it or dummy pills, mostly for 3 months, usually with counselling as well.
About 46 in 100 on naltrexone went back to heavy drinking, against 54 in 100 on dummy pills. It helped less, if at all, with stopping completely.
People on naltrexone drank on about 5 fewer days in every 100. Feeling sick, dizziness and vomiting were more common.
When compared directly, naltrexone and acamprosate did about the same, but most people in that comparison were in one trial.

item.statement: In old trials, benzodiazepines made seizures during alcohol withdrawal much rarer.
item.why: About 1 in 100 people on a benzodiazepine had a seizure, against about 8 in 100 on dummy pills, and delirium was less common too. The trials ran from the 1960s to 1983, and few people had seizures.

lines.short: In old trials, benzodiazepines cut seizures: about 1 in 100, against 8 on dummy pills.
lines.but: The trials were from the 1960s to 1983, and few people had seizures.
how: Benzodiazepines are calming medicines. Old trials gave them or dummy pills to people going through alcohol withdrawal.
About 1 in 100 people on a benzodiazepine had a seizure, against about 8 in 100 on dummy pills. Delirium was also less common: about 2 in 100 against 6.
Other medicines were not clearly better or worse. One kind of antipsychotic given on its own was followed by more seizures and delirium than benzodiazepines.
Few trials looked at people who already had the DTs.

item.statement: Ketamine's two mirror-image forms, S and R, have the same effects.
item.why: In one study of ten healthy people, the S form raised scores for hallucinations and a changed sense of self in all ten, while the R form brought relaxation. Everyone could tell when they'd been given a drug.

lines.short: In one small study the S form caused psychosis-like effects; the R form did not.
lines.but: Only ten people took part, and everyone could tell when they had been given a drug.
how: Ten healthy people had the S form, the R form and a dummy, a month apart.
On the S form, all ten scored higher for hallucinations and a changed sense of self.
On the R form, the same people described relaxation, and their brain scans moved the other way.
The ordinary mix of the two forms was never given to these same ten people.

item.statement: In a lab study, people's thinking was clearly worse the day after LSD.
item.why: In 24 people, a few memory and word tests went a little better the next morning and one rule-switching puzzle a little worse, which may just be chance. The report gave no mood or sleep data.

lines.short: A few small changes, some better and some worse, which may just be chance.
lines.but: One study of 24 people after one small lab dose; this report gives no mood or sleep data.
how: People took LSD on one day and a dummy drink (placebo) on another, in random order.
The next morning, a few memory and word tests went a little better after LSD.
One card-sorting puzzle about switching rules went a little worse after LSD.
The researchers checked many scores without allowing for that, so some differences may be luck.

item.statement: People who use meth report much more low mood than people who use other drugs.
item.why: Against people who use other drugs, there was no clear difference. Against people who don't use meth, low mood was somewhat more common, and things like a hard life may explain part of that.

lines.short: People who use meth report low mood somewhat more often than people who don't.
lines.but: Other differences, such as using other drugs or a hard life, may explain part of it: against people who use other drugs, there was no clear difference.
how: Across 6 studies, after allowing for some other differences, the odds of low mood were about 1.3 times higher.
Most studies measured symptoms, not diagnosed depression.
Two studies that followed people over time, allowing for how they felt before, found about 1.5 to 1.6 times the odds.
Among people who use other drugs, those who used meth did not report clearly more low mood.

item.statement: People with regular or problematic meth or amphetamine use died nearly 7 times as often as others their age.
item.why: That's about 1 in 90 a year, in studies of people in treatment, in hospital or justice records, or who inject, not everyone who uses. Many also used opioids, so not all of it is the drug.

lines.short: Among people with regular or problematic use, about 1 in 90 died each year.
lines.but: These were people in treatment, in hospital or justice records, or who inject, not everyone who uses. Not all of it is the drug.
how: In studies of people with regular or problematic use, about 1 in 90 died each year.
That is nearly 7 times the rate of people of the same age and sex.
Overdose deaths were about 25 times as common; suicide and homicide about 12 times. These figures are less certain.
Many also used opioids or injected, so this does not show how much is due to the drug itself.

item.statement: In one study, people dependent on meth reported more violent crime in months they used it.
item.why: It was about 12 in 100 months with meth use, against 3 in 100 without, comparing each person with themselves. But use and crime were reported for the same months, so which came first is unclear.

lines.short: Two long-term studies linked meth use to more violence. This held after other things were counted.
lines.but: Both studies share authors, and neither could show which came first.
how: A review of mostly weak studies found the link shrank and became unclear once other things were counted.
In New Zealand, about 1,000 people followed from birth reported somewhat more violence in times they used meth or speed. This held after other things were counted.
In Australia, 469 people dependent on meth reported violent crime in 12 of 100 months with meth use and 3 of 100 without.
That study compared each person with themselves. But people reported use and crime for the same months.

item.statement: Children on the ADHD medicine methylphenidate had trouble falling asleep far more often than on a dummy pill.
item.why: Across 35 trials, it was recorded nearly three times as often with the medicine, though who recorded it changed how big the gap looked. A drug company paid for the review.

lines.short: Children on methylphenidate had sleep problems recorded more often than children on a dummy pill.
lines.but: The review says how many times more often, not how many children out of 100.
how: A review combined 35 trials in children and teenagers with ADHD.
Trouble falling asleep was recorded nearly three times as often with the medicine as with the dummy pill.
Who recorded sleep problems, and whether a questionnaire was used, changed how big the difference looked.
A drug company paid for the review, and two of the authors work for its parent company.

item.statement: A death record can say morphine even when the person took heroin.
item.why: In the body, heroin quickly turns into morphine, and some death records named morphine or mixed drugs instead. In the places studied, closer reviews linked more deaths to heroin than the records did.

lines.short: In the places studied, closer reviews linked more deaths to heroin than records did.
lines.but: Each review used its own rules for what counts as a heroin death.
how: In the body, heroin quickly turns into morphine. Some death records said morphine or mixed drugs instead of heroin.
In Maryland (2012 to 2015), certificates named heroin in about 52 in 100 of the deaths a fuller review linked to heroin.

In Victoria, Australia (2012 to 2013), about 34 in 100 deaths a review linked to heroin lacked the heroin code in national figures. A few deaths coded as heroin were judged to involve it only by chance.
In England and Wales, an estimate came out about half as large again as the official count. It mixed heroin with morphine and did not match each death.

item.statement: Scans of people with vision problems after poppers mostly showed damaged light-sensing cells at the back of the eye.
item.why: People described blurry or dim vision in the middle; of those scanned again, about 6 in 10 showed the damage improving or clearing. These are reports of about 113 people, so they can't prove poppers caused it or show how often it happens.

lines.short: It seems so, in some people: reports describe blurry central vision and damage at the back of the eye.
lines.but: These are uncontrolled reports of people who saw an eye doctor, so they cannot prove poppers were the cause, or show how often it happens or which poppers do it.
how: Doctors in at least 12 countries have written about 113 people with eye problems after poppers, some after using them once.
Most had both eyes affected: blurry or dim vision in the middle, flashes of light, or a blank spot.
In most people scanned, the scans showed damage to the light-sensing cells at the centre of the retina, at the back of the eye.
Of the people who had a second scan, about 6 in 10 showed the damage improving or clearing.
